articles.summary: DiffusionGemma is an experimental open-weight language model that uses discrete diffusion to generate text at exceptionally high speed by iteratively refining blocks of 256 tokens in parallel, avoiding the sequential decoding bottleneck of conventional autoregressive large language models. This approach enables the model to achieve around 20 tokens per forward pass and 1,500 output tokens per second on a single NVIDIA H100 GPU, significantly faster than AR models. DiffusionGemma also retains the starting model's support for thinking mode, multimodal inputs, and long contexts, suggesting a path toward hybrid diffusion-AR decoding.

The malicious versions of arrayref and append-only-vec crates have been removed from crates.io, and the crates involved are no longer available for inspection.

articles.title: Reclaim the terminal
articles.summary: The terminal is not always the same, even when a program is piping input to it. The terminal's fd 0 and fd 1 are connected to different processes, and the shell only launches the whole pipeline at once. This means that each stage of the pipeline can read from its own stdin, and the next stage can start reading from the previous stage's pipe. This is possible because the binary itself is piping input to itself, and the shell only needs to know which stage is currently reading from stdin.

articles.title: Why I still hand write my commit messages
articles.summary: Writing detailed Git commit messages is still a valuable use of time for developers, even in a world where Large Language Models can write them for you. This practice helps explain why changes are made, which is crucial for understanding the context and potential implications of those changes. By documenting the reasoning behind a change, developers can ensure they understand the changes and can explain them in their own words, which can be particularly beneficial when reviewing changes or explaining them to others. This practice also helps to promote a blame culture, where developers are more likely to take responsibility for their changes and understand the reasoning behind them.

articles.title: A theory for decades of C vulnerabilities
articles.summary: A semantic invariant is a property that must remain true about a value, object, or relationship throughout the execution of a program if the program is to continue operating on the intended data and memory. This concept is central to the theory of C vulnerabilities, which are often understood as different failure manifestations of broken semantic invariants. The difficulty is that standard C does not make these relationships part of the types of the values that carry them, and the result is not simply that C contains "unsafe operations" but rather a broader family of security vulnerabilities that can be understood as different failure manifestations of broken semantic invariants.
